title: Augustine of Canterbury
hook: sent from Rome to England, he's told: don't destroy their temples, bless them

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory, the pope who signed himself servant of servants. Who did you serve without telling anyone? Day seven hundred ninety.

On the road, they lose their nerve. A group of monks has left Rome on Gregory's orders, headed for the far island of the English. On the road they start to talk. Bede, who tells the story, says they were struck with fear: a fierce, unbelieving people, a language none of them could speak. So they stop, and send their leader back to Rome to ask the pope to call the whole thing off. Their leader is a monk named Augustine. Not the Augustine of the Confessions; another Augustine. Gregory sends him back with a letter that says, more or less, keep going. It would be better not to start a good work than to turn back from it. So they go on.
screen: `ON THE ROAD, THEY LOSE THEIR NERVE.`
`ASK THE POPE TO CALL IT OFF.`

segments.voice: They land in Kent, and the king, Ethelbert, comes to meet them. Bede says he insisted on meeting them out in the open air, in case they tried some kind of magic indoors. The monks walk up carrying a silver cross and a picture of Christ painted on a board, singing as they come. The king listens, and his answer is careful and fair. Your words are good, he says, but they're new to me, and I can't just leave what my people have always held. But you've come a long way. Stay. We'll feed you, and you can speak to anyone who will listen. Later, Gregory writes a letter about what the monks should do with the old temples of the English. Bede keeps it. Gregory says he has thought about it for a long time. Don't tear the temples down. Take out the idols, bless the buildings with water, set up altars, and let them become places of worship to God. That way, he says, people can keep coming to the places they already know. Even their old feast days should become feasts of thanksgiving. And then a sentence about how people change: whoever wants to climb a high place goes up step by step, not in leaps. Two cautions. Bede also keeps an earlier letter in which Gregory urged the king to overthrow the shrines, so this was a change of mind, not his only word. And it was still a mission: the old gods' images were removed. But in the later letter Gregory chose to keep what he could: the buildings, the gathering places, the habit of feasting together.

Here's the practice: honor what's good in a place. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place you've been trying to change. A team at work. A family habit. A neighborhood. A room in your own house. Before you think about what's wrong with it, find one thing that's already good there. A gathering. A tradition. A person who keeps it going. Let yourself see it clearly. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just name it to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Augustine. The monk who nearly turned back, reached Kent, and carried Gregory's advice: keep the old places, and bless them.
Your line: bless, don't destroy. Today, in the place you named, say the good thing out loud to someone before you suggest any change. Day seven hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Anglican and Catholic Christians remember Augustine of Canterbury as the monk sent by Gregory to Kent, and the archbishop of Canterbury's chair is traditionally called the chair of Saint Augustine.

fork.setup: you're one of the monks on the road from Rome. you're afraid of the people ahead and you don't speak their language. what do you do?
options: stop, and send your leader back to ask the pope to cancel.
fork.reveal: they stopped and sent Augustine back to Gregory. Gregory sent him back with a letter: better not to start a good work than to turn back from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary who knocked down the old religion.
what it means: a monk who nearly turned back, and a pope who told him to keep the old places and bless them.
what a scholar hears: Gregory's letter in Bede: remove the idols, keep the temples, turn the feasts to thanksgiving, and climb by steps, not leaps.

notes: The index hook gives the year 597; the script states no date, per the claims rule. Confirm.

Bede 1.23: monks afraid of a 'barbarous, fierce and unbelieving nation' whose language they did not know; Augustine sent back; Gregory's letter ('better not to begin a good work than to turn back'). Paraphrased; confirm.
Bede 1.25: Thanet landing, Ethelbert meets them in the open air for fear of magic, silver cross and image of Christ painted on a board, the king's answer. Paraphrased; confirm.

Bede 1.30 (letter to Mellitus): temples kept, idols destroyed, holy water, altars, feasts turned to thanksgiving, 'steps, not leaps'. Note that Bede 1.32 (Gregory's letter to Ethelbert) urges overthrowing the shrines; the script doesn't address the tension. A Keeper may want a line on it.
The script says honestly that the idols were still removed; confirm the framing is fair to the pre-Christian English.
howItsDone: 'chair of Saint Augustine' for Canterbury's archiepiscopal throne; confirm.
Editor: 'the famous one' replaced with 'the Augustine of the Confessions'; stock line about a sentence 'that works for anyone' reworded.
Editor (second pass): 'halfway' changed to 'on the road' in hook, screen and match; Bede says only that they were seized with fear on the journey.

Audit: the teach presented the letter to Mellitus (1.30) as Gregory's whole policy; it now notes the earlier letter to Ethelbert (1.32) urging the shrines be overthrown, and calls 1.30 a change of mind. The usual dating puts 1.30 after 1.32 (both 601); Keeper to confirm. Stock opener 'It's worth being honest' (also used on day 785) cut. Orthodox dropped from howItsDone (unconfirmed).
